claim: Visual scene memory processing by the upstream structures of the hippocampus is largely unknown.
source: How visual scene memory is processed differentially by the upstream structures of the hippocampus is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, representing a gap in understanding.

claim: When rats made spatial choices in a T-maze using visual scenes displayed on LCD screens, the inactivation of the MEC but not the LEC produced severe deficits in performance.
source: When the rat made spatial choices in a T-maze using visual scenes displayed on LCD screens, the inactivation of the MEC but not the LEC produced severe deficits in performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the SSC task showing differential effects of MEC vs LEC inactivation.

claim: When the task required the animal to push a jar or to dig in the sand in the jar using the same scene stimuli, the LEC but not the MEC became important.
source: However, when the task required the animal to push a jar or to dig in the sand in the jar using the same scene stimuli, the LEC but not the MEC became important.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the SNSC task showing differential effects of LEC vs MEC inactivation.

claim: The entorhinal cortex is critical for scene-dependent mnemonic behavior.
source: Our findings suggest that the entorhinal cortex is critical for scene-dependent mnemonic behavior, and the response modality may interact with a sensory modality to determine the involvement of the LEC and MEC in scene-based memory tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing that both LEC and MEC are involved in scene-dependent tasks.

claim: The response modality may interact with a sensory modality to determine the involvement of the LEC and MEC in scene-based memory tasks.
source: Our findings suggest that the entorhinal cortex is critical for scene-dependent mnemonic behavior, and the response modality may interact with a sensory modality to determine the involvement of the LEC and MEC in scene-based memory tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double dissociation observed between spatial and nonspatial response tasks.

claim: The visual scene appears to be a strong sensory attribute that functionally recruits the hippocampal system based on human studies.
source: The visual scene appears to be a strong sensory attribute that functionally recruits the hippocampal system based on human studies (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Hartley et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Staresina et al., 2011; Zeidman et al., 2015) and nonhuman primate studies (Gaffan and Harrison, 1989; Wirth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple human studies.

claim: The visual scene appears to be a strong sensory attribute that functionally recruits the hippocampal system based on nonhuman primate studies.
source: The visual scene appears to be a strong sensory attribute that functionally recruits the hippocampal system based on human studies (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Hartley et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Staresina et al., 2011; Zeidman et al., 2015) and nonhuman primate studies (Gaffan and Harrison, 1989; Wirth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to nonhuman primate studies.

claim: Memory for the visual scene may function as the linchpin for explaining the involvement of the hippocampus in various cognitive tasks requiring spatial navigation, episodic memory, and imagining future events.
source: Memory for the visual scene may function as the linchpin for explaining the involvement of the hippocampus in various cognitive tasks requiring spatial navigation, episodic memory, and imagining future events [see Maguire and Mullally (2013) for review].
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by a review citation.

claim: Rats were impaired in making behavioral choices using background visual scenes when the dorsal hippocampus was inactivated by muscimol.
source: In our earlier studies, we confirmed that this involvement was also true in rats by showing that rats were impaired in making behavioral choices using background visual scenes when the dorsal hippocampus was inactivated by a GABA-A receptor agonist, muscimol (MUS) (Kim et al., 2012; Delcasso et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies by the authors.

claim: Hippocampal neurons showed significant modulation in the firing rate in a visual scene-dependent manner.
source: In addition, hippocampal neurons showed significant modulation in the firing rate in a visual scene-dependent manner (Delcasso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The functional significance of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) in visual scene-dependent memory is unclear.
source: Despite the significant involvement of the hippocampus in visual scene-dependent memory, the functional significance of its upstream structures, that is, the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC), is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The entorhinal cortex (EC) provides major inputs to the hippocampus.
source: Because the entorhinal cortex (EC) provides major inputs to the hippocampus (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000; Witter et al., 2000; Knierim et al., 2006; Kerr et al., 2007), the EC is expected to play key roles in scene memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The EC is expected to play key roles in scene memory.
source: Because the entorhinal cortex (EC) provides major inputs to the hippocampus (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000; Witter et al., 2000; Knierim et al., 2006; Kerr et al., 2007), the EC is expected to play key roles in scene memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity between EC and hippocampus.

claim: The visual scene has not been considered a key factor in most theories for understanding information processing in the hippocampal system.
source: However, the visual scene has not been considered a key factor in most theories for understanding information processing in the hippocampal system (but see Knierim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of theoretical frameworks in the field.

claim: A majority of recent studies have been guided by a theory that proposed differential functions of the LEC and MEC for nonspatial and spatial memory, respectively.
source: Specifically, a majority of recent studies have been guided by a theory that proposed differential functions of the LEC and MEC for nonspatial and spatial memory, respectively (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Knierim et al., 2006; Henriksen et al., 2010; Ito and Schuman, 2012; Tsao et al., 2013; Van Cauter et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The LEC receives more projections from the perirhinal cortex (PER), an area that is well known for its role in object recognition memory.
source: According to the theory, the LEC receives more projections from the perirhinal cortex (PER), an area that is well known for its role in object recognition memory, and the LEC projects to the hippocampus and subiculum.
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity and functional roles based on established knowledge.

claim: The LEC projects to the hippocampus and subiculum.

evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity based on established knowledge.

claim: The MEC receives most of the projections from the postrhinal cortex (POR), the rodent homolog of the parahippocampal cortex in primates and humans.
source: The MEC receives most of the projections from the postrhinal cortex (POR), the rodent homolog of the parahippocampal cortex in primates and humans, and projects to the hippocampus and subiculum.
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity and homology based on established knowledge.

claim: The MEC projects to the hippocampus and subiculum.
source: The MEC receives most of the projections from the postrhinal cortex (POR), the rodent homolog of the parahippocampal cortex in primates and humans, and projects to the hippocampus and subiculum.
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity based on established knowledge.

claim: It has been hypothesized that LEC-dependent nonspatial memory and MEC-dependent spatial memory are combined as an integrative memory representation within the hippocampus.
source: It has been hypothesized that LEC-dependent nonspatial memory and MEC-dependent spatial memory are combined as an integrative memory representation within the hippocampus.

claim: Physiological studies that have reported differential functions between the LEC and MEC in recent years seemingly support the theoretical framework of nonspatial versus spatial memory.
source: Physiological studies that have reported differential functions between the LEC and MEC in recent years seemingly support this theoretical framework (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Henriksen et al., 2010; Ito and Schuman, 2012; Tsao et al., 2013).

claim: The presence of grid cells in the MEC is believed to provide key evidence in support of the spatial functions of the MEC.
source: For example, the presence of grid cells in the MEC is believed to provide key evidence in support of the spatial functions of the MEC (Hafting et al., 2005), and the cells in the LEC fire in a nonspatial manner (Hargreaves et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on grid cells.

claim: The cells in the LEC fire in a nonspatial manner.
source: For example, the presence of grid cells in the MEC is believed to provide key evidence in support of the spatial functions of the MEC (Hafting et al., 2005), and the cells in the LEC fire in a nonspatial manner (Hargreaves et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a physiological study.

claim: According to the dominant theory, it is implied that the visual scene information is processed by the spatial information processing stream involving the POR and MEC.
source: According to the dominant theory described above, it is implied that the visual scene information is processed by the spatial information processing stream involving the POR and MEC (Knierim et al., 2014).

claim: The POR is characterized as receiving 'visuospatial' sensory information.
source: That is, the POR is characterized as receiving 'visuospatial' sensory information, and the visual scene may belong to this information category (Burwell and Amaral, 1998).

claim: The visual scene may belong to the visuospatial information category.
source: That is, the POR is characterized as receiving 'visuospatial' sensory information, and the visual scene may belong to this information category (Burwell and Amaral, 1998).

claim: Nonspatial information is often characterized based on individual sensory attributes (e.g., olfactory, tactile, and auditory information) from the unimodal and polymodal sensory areas.
source: Because nonspatial information is often characterized based on individual sensory attributes (e.g., olfactory, tactile, and auditory information) from the unimodal and polymodal sensory areas (Burwell and Amaral, 1998) that may be associated more with individual objects than scenes, the existing theory may predict that visual scene-dependent memory is uniquely processed by the spatial information-processing stream involving the POR and MEC, but not the PER and LEC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The existing theory may predict that visual scene-dependent memory is uniquely processed by the spatial information-processing stream involving the POR and MEC, but not the PER and LEC.
source: Because nonspatial information is often characterized based on individual sensory attributes (e.g., olfactory, tactile, and auditory information) from the unimodal and polymodal sensory areas (Burwell and Amaral, 1998) that may be associated more with individual objects than scenes, the existing theory may predict that visual scene-dependent memory is uniquely processed by the spatial information-processing stream involving the POR and MEC, but not the PER and LEC.

claim: This idea might be supported indirectly by behavioral studies testing animals with spatial or contextual memory tasks.
source: Although this idea might be supported indirectly by behavioral studies testing animals with spatial or contextual memory tasks (Majchrzak et al., 2006; Hunsaker et al., 2013; Van Cauter et al., 2013; Morrissey and Takehara-Nishiuchi, 2014), visual scene has hardly been systematically controlled in prior studies that examined the functions of the LEC and MEC.

claim: Sensory and motor components appear to be mixed when existing theories characterize the spatial information stream.

source: For example, if one makes lesions in the POR or MEC and obtains performance deficits in a behavioral task (usually a spatial navigation task), it is difficult to know whether the animal made errors because visuospatial sensory information processing was impaired or because the lesions damaged the response component associated with making spatial choices.

source: The dominant theory seemingly divides the spatial and nonspatial information-processing streams based on the characteristics of sensory information (Burwell and Amaral, 1998; Witter et al., 2000; Eichenbaum et al., 2012), but this division may be an oversimplification of how the brain works.

claim: Both SSC and SNSC tasks are hippocampal-dependent based on prior studies.
source: We used a scene-dependent spatial choice (SSC) task and a scene-dependent nonspatial choice (SNSC) task because, based on our prior studies (Kim et al., 2012; Delcasso et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014), both tasks are hippocampal-dependent but they require spatial and nonspatial responses, respectively.

claim: The SSC task requires spatial responses.
source: We used a scene-dependent spatial choice (SSC) task and a scene-dependent nonspatial choice (SNSC) task because, based on our prior studies (Kim et al., 2012; Delcasso et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014), both tasks are hippocampal-dependent but they require spatial and nonspatial responses, respectively.
